subject: chemistry
source_note: Topic structure follows the CCEA A-Level Chemistry specification. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships (exam boards do not publish these).

units.name: A2 3 — Further Practical Chemistry

connections.why: Electron configuration determines how atoms bond and what charges ions carry
The type of bonding present dictates the giant or molecular structure formed
Bond polarity from electronegativity differences gives rise to dipole and hydrogen-bonding forces
Bonding pairs and lone pairs around an atom set its molecular shape via VSEPR
The mole and reacting-mass calculations underpin titration concentration work
Halogen displacement and oxidising ability are explained using oxidation states and half-equations
Basic mole calculations extend to empirical formulae, gas volumes, yield and atom economy
Titration theory is practised and assessed in the AS3 practical unit
Cation, anion and gas tests are carried out as observational practical work
Van der Waals' forces explain the boiling-point trends of alkanes and their isomers
E/Z geometric isomerism arises from the restricted rotation of the alkene C=C bond
Electrophilic addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes is one route to halogenoalkanes
Alcohols are prepared by nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes with aqueous alkali
IR spectra confirm O-H and C=O groups formed when alcohols are oxidised
Hess's Law cycles in AS energetics are the basis of Born-Haber cycles at A2
Enthalpy alone cannot judge feasibility, so entropy and free energy are introduced
Qualitative collision theory is made quantitative through rate equations and orders
Qualitative Kc work develops into full equilibrium-constant calculations
Equilibrium constants underpin Kw, Ka, pH and buffer calculations
SN1 and SN2 hydrolysis mechanisms link reaction rate to the rate-determining step
Oxidising primary and secondary alcohols prepares aldehydes and ketones
Further oxidation of aldehydes yields carboxylic acids
Carboxylic acids react with alcohols and reagents to form esters and acyl chlorides
Nucleophilic addition of HCN to carbonyls can generate optically active racemic mixtures
IR and NMR are combined with mass spectrometry to elucidate organic structures
Mass spectra and NMR together pin down molecular structure and formula
Redox half-equations underpin iodine-thiosulfate and manganate(VII) titrations
Variable oxidation states and disproportionation explain transition-metal redox chemistry
Standard electrode potentials predict transition-metal redox interconversions
Acyl chlorides and carboxylic acids react with amines and ammonia to form amides
Amino acids combine an amine group with a carboxylic acid group in one molecule
Ester and amide linkages are the basis of condensation polyesters and polyamides
Complexes such as cisplatin, haemoglobin and edta connect transition metals to medicine
Carbonyl preparations and 2,4-DNP derivatives are made in the A2 practical unit
Ligand replacement and hydroxide detection tests are performed experimentally
